source.title: Neuron-based explanations of neural networks sacrifice completeness and interpretability
source.authors: Nolan Dey; J. E. Taylor; A. Wong; B. Tripp; Graham W. Taylor

record.tranche_reason: The study empirically compares neuron-based explanations with a different basis and measures completeness and human interpretability. It bears on the broader question of using neurons as explanatory units, but does not measure the specific claim versions listed.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own AlexNet measurements and comparisons. Results cited from other work are not included as rows. Appendix A also presents per-layer explained-variance plots for ResNet-18, ResNet-50, and ViT-B/16; these plots are not individual neuron-pole job counts or tested activation-prediction scores.
record.test_reason: The study compares the neuron basis with PCA directions in ImageNet-pretrained AlexNet. It uses explained variance, cumulative ablation and a low-threshold human coherence task on the top 16 neurons or PCs per layer. It never assigns jobs to neuron poles or estimates a share of interpretable neurons. It studies no language model, does not examine InceptionV1's polysemantic neurons, and does not vary tools or architecture to see whether neuron interpretability rises. It builds no attribution graphs and does not score explanations by activation prediction. It argues against neuron-based explanation in general, but its results match no listed version, so it is discussion, not a test. The record's 'tests/T2' should be corrected.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is correct. Add that small-eigenvalue PCs are uninterpretable yet still affect accuracy when ablated. Add that the authors recommend population-level bases over neurons for networks like AlexNet.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares PCA and neuron bases using activation-variance measurements, cumulative ablations, and a human visualization task. It does not label neuron poles by jobs or test explanations against held-out activating examples.
record.method_sensitivity: Layer changes the results: conv1 is an exception in the ablation comparison; conv4 and conv5 show a change in relative ablation impact after about 50 high-variance PCs; the PCA-neuron interpretability gap is especially pronounced in conv2, fc1, and fc2 and less so in fc3. Interpretability also declines for deeper convolutional layers.

fits_no_version.finding: In AlexNet, activation variance is far more concentrated in top PCs than in neurons; for fc1, 42 PCs versus 2782 neurons reach 80% variance. conv4 and conv5 need similar counts at 99%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In standard CNNs, activation variance is concentrated in a few principal components rather than in individual neurons.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating high-variance PCs hurts accuracy faster than ablating high-variance neurons, except in conv1. In conv4 and conv5 the order flips after about 50 ablations. Low-variance PCs matter little.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For AlexNet, top PCs carry more of the network's function than top neurons in most layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Participants recognized coherent transitions more accurately for PC visualizations than for neuron visualizations, F(1,21)=34.50, p<.001. Authors describe neuron visualizations from conv3 to fc3 as semantically meaningless. This is related to V4's interpretable-neuron share but uses an old architecture, one tool and no share estimate.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In AlexNet, top-variance neurons beyond conv1 are less human-interpretable than top PCs under nearest-neighbour visualization.

record.problems: The main completeness and user-study comparison is limited to AlexNet pretrained on ImageNet. The authors describe their interpretability task as a low threshold: participants needed to identify a coherent transition, not explain its meaning. Several layer-specific values are shown only in figures. The paper studies only the forward pass.
record.rows_left_out: The paper also plots per-layer explained-variance curves for ResNet-18, ResNet-50, and ViT-B/16 in Appendix A, Figures 8-10. Those additional layer-level figure-only outcomes are not included here; the text gives a qualitative aggregate description that variance is more concentrated in PCs for all networks studied. Low-variance neuron-versus-PC ablation curves beyond the aggregate textual result are also not itemized layer by layer.

untested.parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole job shares (~90% one job, ~7% two, 2–4% not understood); no language model or pole labelling.
Shares across dense and MoE language models and scale; only vision models (AlexNet; variance-only plots for ResNet-18/50, ViT-B/16).
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose, recursive generalization versus superposition.

Effect of architecture, regularization or better tools on the share of interpretable neurons; InceptionV1-sized estimates. AlexNet neurons are tested with one tool only, as human coherence accuracy on top-16 neurons, not as a share.
Neuron-based attribution graphs explaining behaviour without a replacement model.
Whether explanations from activating examples predict firing on held-out inputs.
Automated simulation scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Neuron versus PC comparisons use only the top 16 basis vectors per layer, with a low interpretability threshold (detecting order, not naming meaning). Figure 5 annotates 80% and 99% basis counts per layer that rows R1–R5, R7 and R8 could record numerically, but these rows link to no version. The record's version statuses (all not_tested) are right; only the relation and tranche are changed.

versions.untested_parts: Does not assess neuron poles, assign jobs to poles, or estimate the share with one or multiple jobs.
Does not estimate shares of poles with named jobs across models or sizes, or test scaling to trillions of parameters.
Does not test InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose, recursive generalization, or superposition.
Does not attribute messy neurons to architecture, regularization, or tools, or estimate the share of interpretable neurons for InceptionV1-sized models.
Does not build attribution graphs or test whether they explain behavior without a replacement model or reconstruction error.
Does not test whether explanations written from activating examples predict activation on held-out examples.
Does not use automated activation simulation on new text to score neuron explanations.

rows.subject: 22 user study participants evaluating AlexNet visualizations
rows.operation_detail: Post-hoc factorial ANOVA compared visualization basis and layer for fully connected layers.
rows.measure: Participant accuracy recognizing coherent transitions
rows.value: Basis effect: F (1,21) = 32.91, p < .001; layer effect: F (2,42) = 4.01, p < .05; interaction: F (2,42) = 8.95, p < .001
rows.note: The basis difference was pronounced in fc1 and fc2 but less so in fc3.

rows.subject: 22 user study participants evaluating AlexNet visualizations
rows.operation_detail: Post-hoc factorial ANOVA compared visualization basis and layer for convolutional layers.
rows.measure: Participant accuracy recognizing coherent transitions
rows.value: Basis effect: F (1,21) = 9.32, p < .001; layer effect: F (4,84) = 10.66, p < .001; no significant interaction
rows.note: PCA was favored over neurons, and shallower-layer visualizations were more interpretable than deeper-layer visualizations.
